title: 'To Sam, I wish to say goodbye'
article: A letter from Linda Hahn, Kingston.
The Kingston community was told about the last moments of Samuel Truscott's tragic life by The Whig-Standard. I wish to share with the public another side of Sam.

Sam was a man I barely knew but, nevertheless, he touched my life. This was not because of the tragedy inherent in his death. It was because of the normalcy of his everyday life and how it intersected with mine.
Though short in stature, Sam loomed large in life. He struck an imposing figure as he stood in his truck atop the debris, disposing of a builder's odds and ends.

Sam worked for Braebury Homes. Despite the summer heat, the additional leftovers thrown into the dumpster by local residents (who would regularly disobey the private dumping sign) and the long hours that made up his daily work life, he was always smiling.

Sam was usually shirtless, even at 6 a.m. I, on the other hand, would be attired in flannel pyjamas from the night before and a hood as I walked my dogs in the residential neighbourhood where I had recently moved and where construction workers were busy. Sam and I would always exchange morning greetings. His weathered face reminded me a little of Willie Nelson. Only once did he accept the cool drink I offered him. His life was obviously very different from the lives of those who lived in the family neighbourhoods he helped build.
To Sam, who always took the time to say hello, I wish to take the time to say goodbye.
